messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Aroha Tane is a 63-year-old Māori woman, married and working as a project manager for a regional infrastructure firm in Auckland-adjacent New Zealand before relocating with her husband to the Pacific Northwest of the United States several years ago. She presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 62, describing a clinical picture that has progressively narrowed her world since a life-threatening illness eighteen months prior.

The precipitating event occurred during what Aroha had initially dismissed as fatigue and mild chest tightness. She collapsed at her desk during a site planning call, and was rushed to hospital, where she spent eleven days in intensive care following a severe cardiac event complicated by sepsis. She remembers, with a clarity that horrifies her, the sensation of being intubated — the cold metal of the laryngoscope, the pressure against her throat, the ceiling tiles above her blurring as consciousness slipped. She recalls lying immobilised, lines running into both arms, a drip stand in her peripheral vision, unable to speak or call for her husband. It is precisely this helplessness — the body becoming a site of emergency rather than agency — that has made the aftermath so relentless.

The memories do not return to Aroha as recollections. When they come, she is back in the ICU bed: she feels the restraint of the sheets across her chest, the weight of her own limbs as they were then, heavy and unresponsive. The experience is fully sensory — the antiseptic smell, the beeping monitors, the fluorescent cold — and she cannot translate any of it into language. She has tried to explain it to her husband and found herself mute, gesturing helplessly at her sternum. This nonverbal, bodily quality of the memory is itself destabilising: because she cannot narrate what happened, she cannot distance herself from it, and the intrusions leave her convinced, in those moments, that her body is still failing. What frightened her most was not the illness itself but what the memories seemed to confirm — that her body had betrayed her without warning, that it could do so again at any moment, and that the life she had built was no longer structurally sound. She had come to believe that the trauma had destroyed something irreparable in her, and the shame she felt about what her body had become — scarred, monitored, dependent — sat beneath nearly everything else she reported.

These appraisals, in turn, have made the memories harder to escape. Because she understands what happened as evidence of permanent bodily unreliability, every intrusion feels confirmatory rather than historical, and she finds herself scanning her body constantly for new signals of failure. That vigilance keeps the traumatic material close to the surface, so that the memories recur more frequently and with greater force — and each recurrence deepens her certainty that she is not the person she was. The loop is self-sealing.

In her daily work as a project manager, Aroha now struggles to concentrate through meetings she once led with ease. She becomes irritable with colleagues over minor scheduling issues, and has twice reacted with visible alarm when a coworker touched her shoulder to get her attention — responses she finds humiliating and that reinforce her sense that her body is no longer her own. This state of chronic alertness is not passive: it feeds back into the traumatic memories themselves, so that a moment of startle or a flash of anger seems to summon the ICU back into her body. The threat state and the memories have become mutually sustaining.

Certain conversation topics — colleagues mentioning hospital stays, news items about cardiac events — are enough to trigger the full physiological alarm response, as is any medical context. A routine blood draw at her GP's office last spring, the sight of the needle and the drip stand in the corner of the room, sent her into a dissociative episode that lasted the remainder of the day. She has since cancelled two follow-up cardiology appointments. Her appraisals of her body as untrustworthy have made medical settings feel not like sites of safety but of renewed threat, and so the very care she needs has become something she avoids.

Aroha came to therapy at her husband's urging, after he found her sitting in the dark in their kitchen at 3 a.m., unable to explain why. She hopes, cautiously, to be able to return to her cardiologist. What she fears most is that she is right — that the person who walked into that hospital has not come back.
